task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-08-08, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: Can cut-heavy versus drive-heavy classification be defined from play-by-play without using the outcome being tested?
With 24 units, what minimum detectable difference in regular-season-to-playoff change is achievable?
Is the transfer measured within unit (same team or player across contexts) rather than by comparing unrelated groups?
Are cut and drive shares stable enough across seasons to serve as stable exposures?
Does the result survive placebo play types and control for shot quality, pace, opponent and playing time?

historical_evidence.finding: Team-level (team, PT, context) cells with min 30 possessions across up to 25 teams. DRIVE PPP was 1.198 in regular season vs 0.912 in playoffs (-0.286); PNR -0.173; PULL_UP +0.301; others within -0.07. No CIs recorded. Validation status: no_validation_recorded. Record notes it motivated a playoff DRIVE exclusion and a proposed playoff DSI offset.

Season stability of top sequential suppressors: only 2/30 stars (7%) had a stable top suppressor (>=75% same across seasons). Sample 30 stars x 4 seasons, min n=20/cell. Classified as B_powered_null. Validation status: no_validation_recorded.

BEST-AVOID gap was +0.620 (MW p=0.0000, n=2,544 rows, 272 games). Excluding CUT>15% games gave +0.625; only 4/272 games had CUT>15%, so that subgroup (n=36) was too sparse to be informative. Same-pipeline validation only.

Rank-1 openers were CUT-centered and exceeded stretch ceilings by +9.6 to +15.9pp for every team; attributed to an optimizer that ignores personnel feasibility. Limited by small sample; risks recorded as BASE_RATE, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY and SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using season-to-season stability of a player's top sequential suppressor as evidence of a stable role.
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as a powered null: only 2/30 stars met the 75% stability rule, so role-level stability was not established under that rule.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Optimizer recommendations that were CUT-centred without checking whether the top-8 rotation could sustain them.
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as artifact: the optimizer ignored personnel, so CUT targets were 3-10x the stretch ceiling in every team-game. The lesson is that feasibility constraints must be built into any role-based comparison.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating the CUT-heavy subgroup as a basis for conclusions about the gap.
failed_approaches.why: Only 4 of 272 games had CUT>15% (n=36 rows), so the subgroup was too sparse to estimate the effect; its exclusion changed the gap only trivially.

evidence_establishes: A team-level regular-season-to-playoff comparison of play-type PPP ([prior work][prior work]) recorded a DRIVE decline of about 0.29 points per possession. This is the only retrieved record that speaks to drive-heavy play transferring across contexts.
Play-type efficiency can change materially between regular season and playoffs, so context transfer is a real concern and cannot be assumed away.
Season-to-season stability of individual sequential patterns is low under a strict rule ([prior work][prior work]), so exposure measures need stability checks before they are used as role labels.
Team-game optimizer outputs that ignore personnel feasibility can create apparent role effects (FAM:[prior work]), so any role-based result needs a feasibility check.
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record compares cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers, so none tests whether cut-heavy roles travel better.
No retrieved record reports cut share or cut-heavy classification with a stated reliability.
[prior work][prior work] has no CIs and no validation, so the size of its DRIVE effect is not established with confidence.
[prior work] do not show whether the 24 units in this task are the same teams or players as those in the retrieved records.
own_inferences: The question is most naturally tested as an interaction: whether the regular-season-to-playoff change in efficiency differs between cut-heavy and drive-heavy units. That is a different estimand from the one reported in [prior work][prior work].

With n=24 units, only large differences in transfer are detectable. A transfer gap of the size seen for DRIVE in SF-[prior work] would be near the [source] of detectability if the gap were split across two groups of about 12.
Cut and drive shares are likely to be correlated with team style, roster and playing-time mix, so their effects on transfer are confounded unless these are modelled.
uncertainties: The unit count discrepancy: the task says n=24 units, while [prior work][prior work] used up to 25 teams. The unit definition (team, player or team-context) is not clear.
The date ranges and playoff sample sizes for each season are not given in the retrieved records. The 2025-26 playoffs were recorded as complete only from 2026-06-21.
The exact definitions of cut-heavy and drive-heavy in the data catalog are not known from retrieval. The glossary and data_catalog were not consulted.
Whether shot-distance and play-type labels are reliable across seasons is not established.
No validation was recorded for [prior work][prior work] or [prior work][prior work].

historical_effect.explanation: [prior work][prior work] showed that DRIVE efficiency drops materially from regular season to playoffs, which makes the drive-heavy side of the question plausible and suggests that transfer should be tested within unit rather than assumed. [prior work][prior work] and FAM:[prior work] showed that role stability and personnel feasibility can fail or produce artifacts, so the design needs a stability check and a feasibility control. Together these moved the decision from a direct test to a narrower, pre-specified test with an explicit power caveat. They do not show that the cut-versus-drive comparison has been done.

blocking_constraints.text: With 24 units split into cut-heavy and drive-heavy groups, only large transfer gaps are detectable. Power must be computed before analysis.
Cut and drive shares must be shown to be stable across seasons (cf. [prior work][prior work], where strict stability failed for 28/30 stars).
Playoff possession counts per unit may be too low for stable play-type PPP (cf. the 30-possession minimum in [prior work][prior work]).
Team style, roster and playing time may drive both the cut/drive mix and the transfer outcome.

prior_work.summary: [prior work][prior work] is the closest prior work: it compares regular-season and playoff PPP by play type and finds a recorded DRIVE decline (supported, no CIs, no validation). It does not classify units as cut-heavy or drive-heavy and does not test whether those roles transfer. [prior work][prior work] and FAM:[prior work] bear on role stability and feasibility, not on the question as posed. No retrieved record answers the question directly.

risks.text: n=24 units gives low power for a group contrast in transfer; the minimum detectable effect must be stated in advance.
Cut and drive shares may not be stable across seasons or between regular season and playoffs.
Playoff possession counts per unit may fall below the 30-possession minimum used in prior work.
Team quality, pace, roster, shot quality and playing time may confound the cut/drive contrast.
If shaper labels are derived from the same play-by-play used for PPP outcomes, classification and outcome are not independent.
Using playoff data to define the cut/drive label and then testing transfer to the playoffs would leak the outcome into the exposure.
Comparing several play types and contexts raises the risk of spurious findings unless one primary contrast is fixed in advance.
If the result depends on the DRIVE decline seen in [prior work][prior work], placebo play types must show no comparable pattern.
Play-style and rule changes across 2022-23 to 2025-26 may shift cut and drive frequencies over time.
Play-type and shot-distance labels from the NBA stats API may be misclassified, which would blur the cut/drive distinction.

design.estimand: Difference between cut-heavy and drive-heavy units in the change in points per possession from regular season to playoffs (transfer gap), with the regular-season classification fixed in advance.
design.unit: Team-season (or team-context) unit with at least 30 possessions in each context; player-level analysis only as a sensitivity check.
design.sample: Units from the NBA 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular seasons and playoffs, plus 2025-26 once complete. Freeze the data and state the number of units in each group; resolve the 24-versus-25 unit discrepancy first.
design.power: Compute the minimum detectable transfer gap at 80% power for the expected group sizes before analysis. Report it. If it exceeds the effect size in [prior work][prior work], report the test as underpowered.
design.controls: Shot quality (expected points by shot location), pace, opponent strength, playing time and roster-level usage. Use a mixed model with unit random effects. Classify cut and drive shares on one season and test transfer on another, so the label is not derived from the outcome.
design.falsification: The hypothesis is falsified if the drive-heavy group shows an equal or larger regular-season-to-playoff change, or if placebo play types (e.g. isolation, spot-up) show a similar gap. Also falsified if the interval includes zero or the sign reverses across seasons.
design.multiplicity: One pre-registered primary contrast (cut-heavy minus drive-heavy transfer gap). All other play types are secondary and reported without correction.
design.decision_rule: Support only if the primary interval excludes zero, the direction holds in a held-out season, and it survives the placebo and control checks. Otherwise report as inconclusive or rejected under the power criterion.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files (play-by-play, rotations, starters, matchup minutes, box score) as of 2026-08-08, with 2025-26 playoffs complete from 2026-06-21. Freeze the snapshot and record the derived play-type graph build version.
